body:
A water level carries a height from one place to another without a line of sight. It works on the principle of communicating vessels: still water in connected tubes open to the air at both ends settles to the same elevation at each end.

Fill a length of clear flexible tubing with water. Hold one end at a reference mark and carry the other end to where you want that height. Once the water is still, its surface in the second end sits at the same elevation as in the first. The tube can bend, sag, turn corners or pass through a wall; its path does not matter, only that the water is continuous and still. That is why it works where an optical level is blocked, and the cited USGS source describes leveling this way across distances up to 30 meters.

Trapped air spoils the reading. The source warns that bubbles cause capillary and head-pressure discrepancies, so the two ends may no longer agree. Remove every bubble before reading; clear tubing lets you inspect the full length for trapped air.

To read it, keep both ends open, wait until the water stops moving, then mark where the water surface sits at each end. Sight both ends the same way so the comparison stays consistent.

summary: Still water in a clear flexible tube open at both ends settles to the same elevation at each end, so it can carry a level mark around corners and through walls where an optical level is blocked. Remove all air bubbles before reading it.
title: Carry a level mark with a tube of water
